title: JavaScript errors versus C# exceptions
hook: Both languages signal failure with throw and try/catch, but C# enforces typed Exception objects and multiple catch clauses. JavaScript accepts any thrown value and handles async failures through promises — a different second channel.

blocks.text: **C# exceptions** are objects derived from `System.Exception`. The **Common Language Runtime (CLR)** unwinds the stack until a compatible **catch** runs or the thread dies. **JavaScript errors** use the same keywords — throw, try, catch, finally — but the language places almost no restrictions on what you throw. TypeScript adds compile-time honesty (`catch (e: unknown)`) without changing runtime. Async C# uses **Task** with await in try/catch; JavaScript uses **Promise** rejections that require **await** or `.catch()` — unhandled rejections are not caught by a bare try around a non-awaited call.

entries.plainDefinition: .NET runtime that enforces Exception types and unwinds the call stack on throw.
entries.example: catch (IOException ex) — CLR matches thrown type

entries.plainDefinition: C# base type for all thrown failures. JavaScript has no single required base — Error is conventional.
TypeScript type for catch parameter — reflects that anything might be thrown at runtime.
C# interface for deterministic cleanup via using. JavaScript uses try/finally or explicit close() — no language using statement.

blocks.text: Engineers moving between C# backends and JavaScript frontends or Node services hit the same bugs: throwing strings in JS because C# would not compile it; forgetting that fetch + promises need await in try; expecting multiple catch blocks in JS. Mapping concepts explicitly — when filter ↔ if inside catch, InnerException ↔ cause, using ↔ try/finally — speeds code review and interview answers.

blocks.title: Same keywords, different guarantees
blocks.body: finally always runs in both languages. Typed catch, when filters, and throw; versus throw ex only exist in C#. JS adds unhandledRejection as a parallel to unobserved Tasks.

items.title: throw new ArgumentException → throw new Error or custom class
items.body: Use Error subclasses and instanceof checks. No compiler enforcement.

items.title: catch (IOException ex) when (...) → single catch + if
items.body: Inspect err.status, err.code, or err.name inside one catch block.

items.title: throw; rethrow → throw err
items.body: Rethrow the same object. Wrap with new Error(msg, { cause: err }) like InnerException.

items.title: using / await using → try/finally with close()
items.body: Call stream.close(), db.release(), or AbortController.abort() in finally.

items.title: Task unobserved → unhandledRejection
items.body: Always await or attach .catch at async boundaries.

diagram.title: C# vs JavaScript failure channels
diagram.source:
flowchart TB
  subgraph CSHARP[C#]
    T1[throw Exception] --> CLR[CLR unwind]
    CLR --> C1[typed catch / when]
    C1 --> F1[finally / using Dispose]
  end
  subgraph JS[JavaScript]
    T2[throw any value] --> SYNC[sync unwind]
    SYNC --> C2[single catch + if]
    C2 --> F2[finally]
    P[Promise reject] --> UR[unhandledRejection if no handler]
  end

blocks.title: Porting C# catch order to JavaScript
blocks.body: Multiple catch blocks for different exception types do not exist in JS. One catch with if/else instanceof branches is the idiomatic translation.

blocks.title: Assuming TypeScript catch types are enforced
blocks.body: catch (e: TypeError) does not make runtime only throw TypeError. Narrow with instanceof like you would treat catch as unknown.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: polyglot teams should document boundary contracts — HTTP APIs return JSON errors; internal JS throws HttpError; C# services throw ProblemDetails-mapped exceptions. Neither language makes Result versus throw free — measure exception rates and rejection counts. C# compiler prevents throw "text"; JS needs lint rules (no-throw-literal ESLint). Cross-language OpenTelemetry links spans across Node and .NET with exception events on both sides. Senior answer: choose throw for invariant breaks and unrecoverable I/O; return Result or error objects for expected validation — in both ecosystems.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Claiming JS and C# exception models are identical. Not knowing JS can throw non-Error values. Missing the async rejection channel. Saying TypeScript enforces catch types at runtime.

interviewTakeaways: C# requires Exception types; JS throws anything — discipline is conventional Error.
C# multiple catch + when → JS single catch with instanceof/if.
InnerException ↔ cause; using ↔ try/finally; unobserved Task ↔ unhandledRejection.
60s: Same keywords, different rules. Typed catch only in C#. await for async. cause and finally map cleanly.
Follow-up: how would you port a C# when filter to JavaScript?
commonPitfalls: Multiple catch blocks in JS — syntax does not exist.
TypeScript catch type annotation trusted at runtime.
Strong answer: 'Map when to if in catch. cause to InnerException. Result/Try for expected in both. await promise errors.'
